where: the Signed-in team card — every roster row, across the full 1152px card
finding: The core view inherits the admin view's four-column grid unchanged (`1fr 10.5rem 7.5rem 6.5rem`), but it has only three things to place and no controls to fill the last column. The 1fr identity cell therefore swells to ~680px to hold ~330px of name and address, and the role chip is left-aligned inside a two-column span it barely occupies. The result is a row split into two clumps with a river of dead space between them and a dead band after them: the name is at the far left edge, the facts about that name are marooned 500px away, and the last 180px of every row is empty. A row that has to be tracked across half a screen is not a row; the reader re-finds their place on every line, and the card reads as an unfinished layout rather than a set table — which is the opposite of the density the desktop is supposed to buy.
evidence: Column 2 starts at x=969 on all eleven rows while the longest email ends around x=530; the role chips end between x=1203 and x=1228 against a card content edge at x=1392. Blurred, the frame is two narrow vertical bands with an empty column down the middle and another down the right.
direction: Stop sharing the admin grid with the read-only view. Either give the core row its own, much tighter column set so identity, recency and role sit as one adjacent group with the trailing column removed, or — since three facts do not need 1152px — cap the card's measure so the columns fill the width they are given. Whichever way, the row must resolve as a single object at a glance, and no column should exist that has nothing in it.

where: the role chips and the 'Last seen …' cell in the same rows
finding: Eight of the eleven rows carry an identical grey ringed 'Counselor' capsule, and it is the second-loudest mark in the row after the name — while the recency, which is the one fact that changes line to line and the stated reason a core member opens this screen, is set as the row's quietest text, one contrast step from the email boilerplate above it. The constant is boxed and the variable is not, so the column of chips forms the strongest rhythm in the frame and says nothing. The exception badges ('Never signed in', 'Suspended') also have to compete with eight neighbours wearing the same capsule shape, which blunts them.
evidence: In the blurred frame the right-hand chip column reads at roughly the same weight as the name column; 'Last seen 11 days ago' at ink-400/xs sits between the ink-500 email and the ringed chip in visual weight, i.e. bottom of the row.
direction: Let the majority role stop wearing a box — plain text on the ramp is enough for 'Counselor' — and keep the ringed treatment for the states worth spotting (Admin, Core team, and the warn/danger badges). Then let the recency value step up one notch so it clearly outranks the email it sits beside. No new colour is needed for either move; this is contrast and containment, not hue, and it does not colour staleness.

where: the Active checkbox column in the roster, read against the two exception rows
finding: Ten solid brand-filled ticks stack into the most saturated vertical stripe on the page, and they encode the state that is normal and needs no attention. The two rows that do need attention — Marcus Webb suspended, Hannah Boateng never signed in — are carried by small badges on the left. So the accent is spent on the answer 'everything is fine', repeated ten times, while the news is quiet. Brand is simultaneously doing four unrelated jobs in one frame (wordmark, Admin badge, ten ticks, the Invite slab), and the ticks win on repetition.
evidence: Squint at the frame and the blue dot column and the blue Invite bar are all that survives; the names are a faint grey rhythm and the red and amber badges are the only other survivors.
direction: Bring the majority state down rather than pushing the exceptions up again. The checked mark can sit lower on the ramp and still be unmistakably on — the constraint is that it must not become the near-grey the unchecked box already is, or 'active' and 'suspended' converge. If the native widget will not take that quietly, the alternative is to stop repeating a full-strength accent mark eleven times and let the column read as text with the control appearing on pointer, as the role selects already do.

where: the self row (Dana Ruiz) — the Admin badge and 'Another admin has to change this.'
finding: The badge and its explanation share a two-column span that is narrower than the two of them together, so the sentence wraps beneath the badge and overruns into the access column, starting at the role column's left edge and ending past where every checkbox below it sits. It also lands about 5px below the email's baseline, so the first row of the list has two second lines that nearly, but do not, align. It is the only misaligned thing on the page and it is at the top of the list, which is where the reader calibrates the row pattern.
evidence: The sentence runs from x≈745 to x≈950, crossing the checkbox column edge at x=890; its baseline sits a few pixels under the 'dana.ruiz@example.org' baseline immediately to its left.
direction: Give the note a slot that has a baseline to sit on. Either it occupies the access cell alone, vertically centred where the checkbox it replaces would be and short enough not to wrap, or it drops under the email in the identity cell where a second line already exists. What it should not do is wrap under the badge and align to no column edge in the table.

where: the Suspended badge in the Invited list (wednesday.volunteer@example.org) versus the same badge in the roster (Marcus Webb)
finding: One token, two structural homes on one screen. In the roster the danger badge sits on the name line, where it plainly modifies the person. In the invitation it is appended to the end of the meta line, immediately after 'invited 24 days ago', where it reads as a property of the invitation's age rather than of the address — and it is separated from the unchecked box below that actually states the same thing. The reader has to learn the badge's meaning twice.
evidence: Marcus Webb: name, then badge, on the bold line. wednesday.volunteer: bold address alone on its line, badge trailing the grey 'Counselor · invited 24 days ago'.
direction: Attach the badge to the identity line in both places, so the rule is 'a badge beside a name or address describes that person's access'. The meta line then stays a uniform grey run of role and age across all four invitations.

where: each invitation card's control row (Active checkbox / Withdraw) against the address above it
finding: Inside a narrow stacked card the eye is holding one left edge, and the control row breaks it: the checkbox is indented about 9px past the address's left edge by the label's own padding, and Withdraw's label stops about 16px short of the card's right padding edge for the same reason. Neither edge of the control row lines up with anything above it, so each invitation reads as two blocks loosely stacked rather than one card. The same padding inset is invisible in the roster, where the controls have their own columns; here it has nothing to hide behind.
evidence: Addresses begin at x=1040; the checkboxes begin at x≈1049. The card's content edge is x=1392; 'Withdraw' ends at x≈1376.
direction: Pull the controls' internal padding back out at the card edges — the touch target keeps its size, but the checkbox and the Withdraw label sit on the same left and right edges as the address and meta line above them.

where: the page subtitle under the 'Team' heading
finding: Two sentences set as one unbroken 766px line, roughly 104 characters, which is past the point where a reader tracks reliably back to the next line — and there is no next line only because it happens to just fit. It also aligns to nothing: it stops two pixels short of the invite column, hanging into the gutter between the two cards, while the disclosure prose directly beneath it is capped at a narrower measure. Two adjacent paragraphs of the same size and the same role, set to two different measures, is drift.
evidence: The subtitle spans x=256 to x=1022; the roster card's right edge is x=1000 and the invite card begins at x=1024.
direction: Give the header block one measure and share it with the disclosure paragraph, sized for a comfortable line rather than for the width that happened to be available.
